title: Gator Guides, LLC swamp tours: preparing a chart of accounts and choosing desktop vs. cloud accounting software
participant_role: Accounting software consultant hired by GATOR GUIDES, LLC to prepare a chart of accounts and recommend accounting software
judge_role: Owner of GATOR GUIDES, LLC, a swamp tour company (single-member LLC)
scenario:
You are to assume the role of an accounting software consultant hired by GATOR GUIDES, LLC, a swamp tour company. The owner (judge) wants you to prepare a chart of accounts as the initial software implementation project and also make recommendations related to accounting software applications.

GATOR GUIDES, LLC is a limited liability company with one owner (judge). The company has three revenue sources. The first one includes swamp tours on small airboats, large airboats and pontoons. The second source is snacks, apparel and souvenirs from the swamp store. The third source is photographs from the boats.

The company purchased three small airboats, two large airboats and two pontoons. The airboats were all paid for with cash and are paid in full. The two pontoons were financed, and the company still owes $2,000 on each.

The company leases the swampland used for the tours. They own the mobile home which is used for the main office, ticketing booth and souvenir shop. The company built a deck this year which is a plant asset for the company. The company also has other miscellaneous bills such as utilities, supplies, inventory, etc. which they typically receive terms of n/30.

The company has 15 employees, including guides, ticketing agents, an office manager and a bookkeeper. They contract out a shuttle service which brings the customers out to the swamp. The company also pays a commission to travel agents that promote the swamp tours in tourist areas. The company purchases brochures and pays for billboard and website maintenance. The company accepts cash, credit card, debit card and Apple Pay. From time to time, GATOR GUIDES will contract with large corporate groups to provide tours. In those situations, GATOR GUIDES will bill the corporate client and receive payment in the future.

The owner (judge) wants you to:
1. Use the information provided by the owner (judge) to prepare a chart of accounts (at least 5 accounts) identifying whether the account is an asset, liability, equity, revenue or expense.
2. You will then meet with the owner (judge) to:
   a. Review the chart of accounts
   b. Discuss options for accounting software applications including desktop and cloud computing

You will present your ideas to the owner (judge) in a role-play to take place in the owner's (judge's) office. The owner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented ideas and have answered the owner's (judge's) questions, the owner (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.
tasks: Use the information provided by the owner (judge) to prepare a chart of accounts (at least 5 accounts) identifying whether the account is an asset, liability, equity, revenue or expense
Discuss options for accounting software applications including desktop and cloud computing

solution.overview: A strong answer walks the owner through a chart of accounts organized by asset, liability, equity, revenue and expense, tying each account to a fact in the scenario (airboats and pontoons as plant assets, the $4,000 pontoon note as a long-term liability, accounts receivable for billed corporate tours, three revenue streams with sub accounts). It then explains why the chart is the first step in a computerized system and compares desktop software (more secure, fuller features) with cloud software (continuous updates, mobile access), naming products such as QuickBooks, Sage, Peachtree or FreshBooks.

answer: Assets: Cash, Accounts Receivable (billed corporate groups), Supplies, Inventory (snacks, apparel, souvenirs) as current assets; Small Airboats, Large Airboats, Pontoons, Mobile Home, Deck and Accumulated Depreciation as plant assets (land is leased, so no Land account)
Liabilities: Accounts Payable (n/30 bills) and Payroll Taxes Payable as current; Notes Payable for the pontoons ($2,000 each, $4,000 total) as long term
Equity: Owner's Capital (or Common Stock) and optionally Retained Earnings, since it is a single-owner LLC
Revenue: Tour Income with sub accounts for Small Airboat, Large Airboat and Pontoon; Gift Shop Income with sub accounts for Snacks, Apparel and Souvenirs; Photograph Income
Cost of Goods Sold for store merchandise; Expenses such as Depreciation, Interest, Payroll, Payroll Tax, Commission, Shuttle Service, Utilities, Marketing and Credit Card Fees
Group and number the accounts so the software can produce a general ledger and financial statements

by_task.task: Review the chart of accounts with the owner
answer: The chart of accounts is one of the first things set up in a computerized accounting system
To build it you must understand the company's procedures: type of business, legal format, revenue streams, expenses, assets and liabilities (an environmental scan of the business)
The chart is used every time a business transaction is recorded, and the account names flow to the general ledger and the financial statements
Unused accounts can be deleted and new ones added, but keep the chart broad; transaction detail lives in the accounting records, not in extra accounts

Different transaction types map to different accounts: cash sales to Cash and Tour Income, corporate billings to Accounts Receivable, purchases on n/30 terms to Accounts Payable, card sales create Credit Card Fees

by_task.task: Accounting software options: desktop vs. cloud
answer: Options include QuickBooks, Peachtree, Sage and FreshBooks, most of which offer both desktop and cloud versions
Desktop: data is stored on the company's own computer, generally considered more secure, and desktop versions often have more functionality than the cloud versions
Cloud: software and data live online, updates are continuous and automatic, and the owner, office manager and bookkeeper can access it from a phone or laptop anywhere
Recommend a system that handles inventory for the store, tracks the three revenue streams with sub accounts, processes payroll for 15 employees and accepts card and Apple Pay payments
Whichever is chosen, the bookkeeper should keep business records (invoices, receipts, payroll records, bank statements) organized to support the entries

judge_question_answers.question: What are the benefits of cloud computing?
answer: Continuous, automatic updates so the software is always current
Mobile accessibility: the owner and staff can log in from any device and location, including the ticket booth and the mobile home office
Data is backed up off-site by the provider, and multiple users can work at once
Lower upfront cost with a monthly subscription instead of buying and installing software

judge_question_answers.question: Will the software be difficult to teach my staff?
answer: No; programs like QuickBooks are designed for small business owners and bookkeepers, with menus and forms that look like invoices and checks
Only a few people (bookkeeper, office manager, ticketing agents for sales entry) need training, and each learns just the functions for their job
Vendors offer tutorials, online help and support, and the consultant can provide hands-on training during implementation
A well-built chart of accounts makes daily entry simpler because staff pick from a short, clear list of accounts

key_concepts.definition: The organized list of every account a business uses, grouped as assets, liabilities, equity, revenue and expenses, and usually numbered. It is the first thing set up in accounting software.
Something the business owns or controls that has value, such as cash, accounts receivable, inventory, boats or buildings.

Current assets (cash, receivables, supplies, inventory) will be used or converted to cash within a year; plant assets (airboats, pontoons, mobile home, deck) are long-lived assets used in operations and depreciated.
A debt the business owes, such as accounts payable for n/30 bills (current) or a note payable for a financed pontoon (long term).
The owner's claim on the business: what is left after liabilities are subtracted from assets. For a single-owner LLC it is usually tracked as Owner's Capital.
Revenue is what the business earns from selling tours, merchandise and photos; expenses are the costs of earning it, such as payroll, commissions, utilities and marketing.
A contra-asset account that collects all depreciation recorded on plant assets; book value = cost - accumulated depreciation.
Net 30: the full invoice amount is due 30 days after the invoice date, with no early-payment discount. Such bills are recorded in Accounts Payable until paid.
Amounts customers owe the business for sales made on credit, such as tours billed to corporate groups and paid later.
Desktop software is installed on the company's own computer (more secure, often more features); cloud software runs online with continuous updates and access from any device.
Gathering information about a business and its surroundings (operations, revenue streams, assets, debts, payment methods) before making decisions such as designing its accounting system.
Source documents such as invoices, receipts, bank statements and payroll records that support each accounting entry and must be kept organized and secure.
